title: Water and plants
summary: How water moves through the plant, how to spot signs of thirst or waterlogging, and how to optimize irrigation to conserve moisture in hot climates.

pages.title: Module overview: water and plants
pages.text:
This module helps you understand how **water** enters, moves through and leaves the plant.

It also teaches you how to optimize the **irrigation** of your crops, how to tell whether a plant has too much or too little water, and how to keep moisture in the soil using simple techniques.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Présentation du module : l’eau et les plantes

pages.title: Water and plants
pages.text: Discover the vital role of **water** in crop nutrition and good practices for preserving soil moisture.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour L’eau et les plantes

pages.title: How does water move through the plant?
pages.text: Let's follow the path of **water**, from the roots to the leaves, to understand how the plant feeds itself and regulates its temperature.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Comment l’eau circule dans la plante ?

pages.title: Transport of mineral elements and trace elements
pages.text:
Water helps carry the **mineral elements** present in the soil, such as **nitrogen (N)**, **phosphorus (P)**, **potassium (K)**, **calcium (Ca)**, **magnesium (Mg)** and **iron (Fe)**.

Water also carries **trace elements** such as boron, zinc and others. These elements play an essential role in **photosynthesis** and other vital functions of the plant.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Le transport des éléments minéraux et oligo-éléments

pages.title: Evapotranspiration and water movement
pages.text:
Water enters the plant through the **roots**. It carries with it the mineral elements present in the soil and rises to the leaves through very fine tubes called **xylem vessels**.

This movement is made possible by a key phenomenon: **evapotranspiration**. Evapotranspiration is the loss of water:

- through the leaves, via tiny openings called **stomata** (this is called **transpiration**);
- and from the soil, in the form of **evaporation**.

When water escapes through the stomata, it creates a suction effect, like a pump. The plant then draws water up from the roots to compensate for this loss: this is what makes water circulate throughout the whole plant.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour L’évapotranspiration et la circulation de l’eau

pages.title: Root pressure and capillarity
pages.text:
Other phenomena support this pumping movement:

- **Root pressure**: it pushes water upward.
- **Capillarity**: it allows water to climb up through the xylem.

This system is essential for the plant to transport the water and nutrients it needs.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Pression racinaire et capillarité

pages.title: The risk of dehydration
pages.text: ⚠️ **Warning**: if **evapotranspiration** becomes too strong (in case of heat, wind or drought), the plant can lose too much water… and become **dehydrated**.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Le risque de déshydratation

pages.title: The plant's leaf is like our skin
pages.text:
In the end, a plant's leaf is a bit like our skin:

- It breathes through tiny invisible openings, like the pores of the skin.
- It lets water out, like sweat. If the air is too dry or hot, it loses too much water, just as we do when we sweat a lot.
- If we are too hot or haven't drunk enough, we become tired: it's the same for the plant!
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour La feuille de la plante, comme notre peau

pages.title: What influences water needs?
pages.text: Not all crops have the same water needs: let's look at the **five factors** that change the amount of water required.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Qu’est-ce qui influence les besoins en eau ?

pages.title: Factors that determine water needs
pages.text:
Water needs depend on:

- **The crop**: some plants need more water than others.
- **The growth stage**: a young seedling needs more water.
- **The soil**: clay soil holds water while sandy soil lets it drain away.
- **The weather**: temperature, wind, air humidity.
- **The presence of mulch**, compost and charcoal in the soil.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les facteurs qui déterminent les besoins en eau

pages.title: How to spot signs of water stress?
pages.text: Learn to observe your plants and your soil to quickly tell a **lack of water** from an **excess of water**.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Comment repérer les signes de stress hydrique ?

pages.title: Too little or too much water: signs to look for
pages.text:
**If the plant lacks water:**

- Soil is dry at depth.
- Leaves are limp, droopy, falling or yellowing.
- Slow growth.

**If the plant has too much water:**

- Leaves wilt even though the soil is wet.
- Unpleasant smell: **rotting or suffocated roots**.
- Fungi or suspicious spots.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Manque d’eau ou excès d’eau : les signes à observer

pages.title: How to water well and keep water in the soil?
pages.text: Let's look at the essential practices to **optimize irrigation** and limit water waste on your growing beds.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Comment bien arroser et garder l’eau dans le sol ?

pages.title: Good watering practices
pages.text:
- **Water in the morning or evening**, never in full sun.
- **Apply mulch** to retain water: straw, dry leaves, husks.
- **Use compost** to keep moisture in the soil.
- **Water sufficiently** so that the soil is moist at depth, not just on the surface.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les bonnes pratiques d’arrosage

pages.title: Why add charcoal to the soil?
pages.text: Discover how **crushed charcoal (biochar)** helps retain water and strengthen soil fertility.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Pourquoi ajouter du charbon dans le sol ?

pages.title: The benefits of biochar in the soil
pages.text:
Crushed charcoal, known as **biochar**, is an excellent ally for:

- **Retaining water**: charcoal works like a sponge, holding water and nutrients in its pores. It stores moisture, then releases it slowly when the soil is dry. It can hold up to **5 times its weight in water**.
- **Feeding the soil (supporting soil life)**: charcoal serves as a refuge for beneficial micro-organisms, such as bacteria and fungi, which help plants feed and strengthen soil life.
- **Strengthening crop resilience**: charcoal improves water retention and soil stability, which helps plants better withstand drought.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les atouts du biochar dans le sol

pages.title: How to use crushed charcoal?
pages.text:
Use **fully cooled charcoal**, finely crushed, as powder or in small pieces of **1 to 10 mm**.

- **If you are making your own compost**: you can add a little charcoal to each layer, alternating it with brown materials (leaves, straw…) and green materials (kitchen scraps, grass clippings…), or mix it in when turning the pile from one bay to the next (see module M3.3.2). Moisten if needed (charcoal is very absorbent) and let it mature.
- **If you already have ready-to-use compost**: add crushed charcoal at a rate of **10 to 20% of the total volume**. For example, for 1 wheelbarrow of compost (80 L), add **8 to 16 L** of charcoal, or about **1 to 2 buckets**. Mix well for even distribution.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Comment utiliser le charbon de bois broyé ?

pages.title: Conclusion: observe and support your crops
pages.text:
**Water** is essential to plant life: it enters through the roots, travels to the leaves and exits through the stomata.

Understanding this path helps you water better, at the right time and in the right amount. With a few simple practices — observing the plant, adapting irrigation, mulching the soil, enriching the compost — you can help your crops grow better, even in dry periods.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Conclusion : observer et accompagner vos cultures
